messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: patched agrad bug
parts:
Woo hoo!

I can't believe auto-dif was running without seg-faulting
before. I'm not used to getting away comparing memory
I shouldn't be looking at. I was starting one past
the end of the stack, which caused an accidental match
due to previous stack detritus (perhaps not so surprising
given the small sizes and 8-byte alignments).

Bottom line is that this (in the derivative propagation):

std::vector<chainable*>::iterator begin = var_stack_.begin();
std::vector<chainable*>::iterator it = var_stack_.end();
for (; (it >= begin) && (*it != vi); --it) ;

should've been this:

std::vector<chainable*>::iterator begin = var_stack_.begin();
std::vector<chainable*>::iterator it = var_stack_.end();
if (begin == it) return; // nothing on stack
for (--it; (it >= begin) && (*it != vi); --it) ;

An embarassing rookie mistake, if I do say so myself.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: patched agrad bug
parts:
If you dig through the LLVM webpage, it has some tools that might help
catch bugs like these. Unfortunately, most of them are for plain C
programs. However, LLVM can input C++ and output "equivalent" C code;
see

http://llvm.org/docs/FAQ.html#translatecxx

From the C code, it looks as if we could use the Clang Static Analyzer

http://clang-analyzer.llvm.org/

or the klee symbolic virtual machine

http://klee.llvm.org/

Also, the SAFEcode project (similar to Valgrind) works directly on C++
but is a mini-fork of LLVM / clang

http://safecode.cs.illinois.edu/

Maybe Jenkins can be configured to do some of these things
periodically?

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: patched agrad bug
parts:
Interesting. We should check some of these
out. I haven't even tried valgrind.

The bug probably would've been caught by
something paying careful attention to memory
access. The subtlety was that I never
dereferenced bad pointers, just compared
them.

Luckily, that's the only place in the program where
we play with memory at all (no other malloc
or new). Though certainly the Boost and Eigen
libs we deal with do a lot under the covers.

The second problem, wasting resources because
of std::numeric_limits<stan::agrad::var> use
in Boost's error checking, wasn't technically
a memory error, so much as unforeseen bad
performance due to programming choice.

- Bob
